gapResults.summary:
The wipe is real when driven end to end, and the damage goes well past the Jobs tab. I ran the real main-sync.gs and saveInventory.gs code over a fake spreadsheet with the 50,000-character cell cap. Against it ran two app sandboxes (the real outbox, retry queue, loadJobs and takeInventorySnapshot) and the real page, where I pressed More ▾ › Snapshot on a 450-line probate desk.

**Variant A (the clear stays when setValues throws).**
- The first batch empties the tab.
- The snapshot's own per-record write in that same batch is answered `ok` with `dropped`, so the pressing device purges that client at once.
- Its first retry, 2 s later, is answered `ok` with every client dropped. That device ends at 0 clients, 0 estimates, plans, hours and manifests, with a green "All changes saved ✓".
- Every other device empties itself at first contact: a save, opening an estimate, the pending-approval watch, or a reload ("Loaded 0 jobs from Sheets ✓").
- The two photographs a device had not yet sent to Drive are deleted with the client.
- No cache survives to rebuild the sheet. A surviving copy is refused as deleted, and even after allowJobRestoreConfirm, opening it empties it before it can save. Only version history holds the clients.
- The server's stores survive the wipe untouched, because the sweep stands down on an empty tab. Once a single new client is typed in, the sweep deletes every other client's estimate, plan, hours and 450-line manifest.
- A device that was offline at its first retry keeps the oversized write. The chip tells the person "do not close or reload the tab", and that device empties the restored tab again.

**Variant B (the clear is rolled back).**
- Nothing is wiped. The device retries forever: 24 failing posts in 10 minutes.
- It is blind to every other device's changes, and reloading it loses the snapshot.

**Further results.**
- One snapshot passes the cap at about 295 named lines. Two snapshots of 150 lines pass it too.
- Two devices each snapshotting 180 to 200 lines pass it at the server's merge, although each record is under the cap. So a size check in the app alone does not prevent it.
- Every result was reproduced with a fresh seed: 450 and 380 lines in the vm, 450 and 360 on the real page.

**What P1 is missing.**
- Never clear the tab before writing it. Check sizes on the merged row, on the server.
- Treat an empty Jobs tab as unread, never as "every client deleted", on the server and in loadJobs.
- Sweep only deletions somebody recorded.
- Never delete unsent photo bytes on a server verdict.
- Treat the size error as blocked, not something to retry.
- Write blob tabs before clearing them.
- A recovery runbook.
- An editor probe (written and tested) to tell variant A from variant B.
works_well: A single-row 'job' write never clears anything: on an intact tab the oversized record fails alone, rows 4 -> 4, 0 clears, in both variants (scenario.js S7, all four runs).

The orphan sweep's own guard holds while the tab is empty: through the wipe and every device's purge, EstimateStore, JobPlanStore, LogStore, MediaStore and ChangeOrderStore keep all three clients' records (scenario.js S1 to S3b: 3/3/3/1/3). So the stores are recoverable from the sheet until a client exists again.

A device booted with the oversized record in its cache posts nothing before loadJobs answers (browser.js C, loadJobs held 15 s: POSTs [] in variants A and B), and loadJobs then replaces the record. So reloading the device that pressed Snapshot cannot re-wipe the tab.

Once the Jobs rows are back with their own ids, the ledger needs nothing. previewDeletedJobs() goes from '3 deleted job id(s)' to '0', loadJobs answers deletedJobs 0, and a reloaded device saves normally (ledger-after-restore.js, 450 and 380).
previewDeletedJobs() is already a one-run diagnosis of the incident: during the wipe it lists every client as deleted.
allowJobRestoreConfirm does let a tab that was open since before the wipe rebuild the rows and estimates from its own copy (recovery.js R2b: sheet back to 3 rows, 3 estimates, the permission spent).
In variant B the unsent photograph bytes survive (photoBytes 1 kept), and the tab is never touched.
measurements: Record size after one real takeInventorySnapshot (threshold.js), 55-character names: 200 lines 34,274 characters; 290 lines 49,592; 300 lines 51,319; 380 lines 64,949; 450 lines 76,867. Two snapshots of 150 lines: 51,219. Real page, 450 lines: record 77,850 characters, saveAllJobs POST 81,554 B.

Variant A, client count per step (sheet / device A / device B), scenario.js A 450, repeated at 380 with the same shape. S0 seeded: 3/3/3. S1 first batch, about 0.25 s after the press: 0/2/3 (A's 'job' write was answered {ok:true, dropped:[J]}). S2 first retry at about 2.25 s: 0/0/3 (answered dropped [J,K,L]; A's badge 'All changes saved ✓'). S3a, B's stale save: 0/0/0 ('Synced ✓', then '3 clients deleted elsewhere'). S3b, B reloads: B's havellin_jobs_v3 = [] ('Loaded 0 jobs from Sheets ✓'). S3c, B adds client N: 1/0/1. S5, rows restored: 4. S5b, A online: no re-wipe (its queue had drained at S2). S6, A reloads: 4.

Variant A, A offline at its first retry (scenario.js A 450 offline and A 380 offline): A holds saveAllJobs for 14 tries ('Failed to fetch'). After the restore (4 rows), A's next retry clears the tab again: Jobs 4 -> 0, 1 clear, 1 cell throw. A reloads to 0. The single-row write is then answered {ok:true, dropped:[J]}.

Variant B (scenario.js B 450 and B 380): sheet 3 throughout. A keeps two writes pending, with 24 failing POSTs and 12 rolled-back clears in 10 minutes. A's refresh does not ask the sheet. On reload, A's cache had the snapshot and loadJobs replaced it (the snapshot is lost; the sheet never had it).

Server stores, variant A: intact at 3 clients until the first new client. After N's estimate, plan, hours and manifest saves: EstimateStore 3 -> 1, JobPlanStore 3 -> 1, LogStore 3 -> 1, MediaStore 3 -> 1 (the 450-line manifest gone). Logger 'Swept records for deleted job(s): <all three>' four times. ChangeOrderStore goes on its next save. Variant B: stores untouched.

Real page, browser.js A 450 and A 360. Calls after the Snapshot press: POST saveAllJobs[3] -> error (cell cap); POST job -> {ok:true, dropped:[9700]}; POST saveAllJobs[3] -> {ok:true, dropped:[9700,9602,9601]}. A's Clients tab reads 'Total Jobs0' by 4.7 s. B, booted afterwards: 0 clients, 0 manifests, its 2 unsent photographs gone, 'Total Jobs0 Active Jobs0 ... Won0'. Zero page errors.

Merge growth (merge-grow.js; A/200, A/180, B/200). Two devices snapshot the same house, records 34,274 and 30,857 characters, each under the cap. The server's per-key merge of invSnapshots pushes the row over: variant A tab 3 -> 0, variant B two writes stuck.

No device cache can rebuild the sheet. recovery.js R2a: a surviving cache's save is answered dropped and the device purges. r2c.js (450 and 380): after allowJobRestoreConfirm, loadJobs still answers deletedJobs 3 of 3, so opening the device empties it before it saves. Only a tab already open since before can push back (R2b).

A whole-file restore after a client was added since (recovery.js R1, 450 and 380): the ledger forgets N, and the device holding N drops it on its next refresh (R1a 'B holds N? false'). It comes back only if that device saves first (R1b 'N on the sheet? true').
The probe (probe.gs, checked by probe-test.js against the fake): variant A logs 'rows left after the failed write: 0', VARIANT A; variant B logs '3 rows still there', VARIANT B.

review.verdict:
If Havellin builds this plan, I would give it the whole-house work: the documented inventory of a Palm Beach house, the disposition record, and the paper trail behind every release. It would not, and should not try to, beat a twenty-year appraiser on the items that carry an estate's tangible value: fine art, fine jewelry, silver, Asian works of art and signed or period furniture.

**Where it would win.** What I use today is a patchwork:
- an auction house's specialist for the top items, who is courting the consignment (the *Kollsman* problem);
- an estate-sale company's tag prices;
- a paralegal's spreadsheet.

None of them gives me every article photographed and numbered by room, a basis on every line, written approval keyed to item numbers, and a ledger that reconciles each line to where it went and what it brought, to the cent. That record is what answers a §733.604(3) request and what protects a trustee under §736.1008(2). The plan's Phase 1 fixes are the right ones, and none of them is optional. As delivered today I could not let a client verify the Court Inventory: it can go FINAL while counting one painting twice, a basis sentence can cite sales that do not exist, and an approval survives a change of destination.

**Where the framing is wrong.** "Better than anyone" cannot mean better than a credentialed, disinterested appraiser under oath for marked artistic or intrinsic value. That is the legal standard on a Form 706 (§20.2031-6(b)) and the evidentiary standard in a dispute. Models are near chance at authenticity (R2 D.1). The agents' honest edge is coverage, speed, a trail of evidence, and a measured error rate on the 90% of lines that are everyday property. The plan should say so, and should send the valuable 10% to the right appraiser earlier.

**What would still stop me signing off.** Five problems sit outside the twenty-eight packs, and each is serious.
1. **Security.** The backend answers anyone who holds its URL, with no sign-in or token. That caller can read every job, including the access codes to vacant houses and where the firearms are, can share any estate folder with any email address, and can trash files. A bank trust department's vendor review would end there, and it breaks the confidentiality of the inventory under §733.604(1)(b).
2. **What the values are.** No engagement term says what Havellin's values are, who may rely on them, or that AI produced them. No named person stands behind a schedule: the paper reads "Prepared by Havellin Palm Beach, LLC".
3. **Independence.** Havellin chooses the selling channel and takes referral fees from the auction houses that sell the lines it values. That is *Kollsman*'s fact pattern. The independence claim in the plan's positioning section is overstated until this is resolved.
4. **Form 706 estates.** Once marked artistic or intrinsic articles total more than $3,000, the app only prints a notice. It does not send those articles under $3,000 each to a sworn appraisal.
5. **Release cautions.** The request carries no caution for the exempt-property window (§732.402), and none for the §20.2031-6(c) pre-sale rule on a 706 estate.

**The accuracy programme.** It is the right idea, but as drafted the "truth" for values is the founders' own opinion. That scores the agents against Havellin's view, not against the market. Publishing a number built that way to trust officers is a representation I would advise against until it rests on realized arm's-length sales and independent appraisals, and counsel has worded it.

**The bottom line.** With Phase 1, the five items above, and the accuracy programme rebuilt on proper truth, I would choose Havellin over my current mix for the inventory and disposition of an estate. I would keep engaging an independent appraiser for the marked artistic and intrinsic items, and Havellin's best pitch is that it gets that appraiser to the right items in the first week.

Professional judgement throughout. The statutes and regulations cited are those the R1 research marks [P]. The 60-day timing rule for qualified appraisals and the §732.402 practice point come from my own background knowledge and should be confirmed.

missing.title: An engagement term that says what Havellin's values are, who may rely on them, and that AI produced them
missing.why:
On a values tier the estate form promises only "a documented asset inventory suitable for use in the court-required filing under §733.604". It does not say that the values are estimates, not appraisals; that they were made from photographs with AI research and checked by staff; who the intended users are; or that reliance by anyone else is excluded.

If a beneficiary later surcharges the personal representative for an undervaluation, the representative will turn to Havellin. The contract will then be silent on the one thing in dispute. Under §736.0807 the fiduciary must use reasonable care in reviewing an agent's work, and that is impossible if they were never told how the work was done.

Nothing records whether the E&O policy being quoted covers value opinions relied on in court filings, or AI-assisted work. Insurers often exclude appraisal services or price them separately.
missing.proposal:
Draft clauses for the counsel bundle, in both forms.
- **The deliverable:** estimates of fair market value at the valuation date, the method, the AI assistance, the review, and the referral to appraisers by rule.
- **Intended users:** the fiduciary and counsel, for the §733.604 inventory and its §733.604(3) explanations.
- **No reliance** by anyone else.
- **Optional contested-matter route:** work engaged through counsel, so drafts and the agents' first answers are prepared at counsel's direction.
- **Consent** to de-identified internal use of photographs and values for quality measurement (see the accuracy item).

Ask Higginbottom in writing whether E&O covers valuation estimates and AI-assisted work. Add that question to the policy-figures reminder Anthony already gets each session.

wrong.item: Ask 11: "You and Ashley settle the truth for the Ellison set" (and the accuracy programme's truth set built on it)
wrong.why:
Identity and value need different truths.
- **Identity** can be settled from evidence: the backstamp in a close-up, a pattern reference, a hallmark. Anthony and Ashley can do that.
- **Value** settled by the founders scores the agents against Havellin's own opinion. The resulting statement would say how often the agents agree with Havellin, not how close they come to the market.

Sixty to a hundred lines also cannot support claims by category and value band.
wrong.fix:
Split the truth.
- Identity truth: settled by evidence, with the source recorded (the backstamp text, the reference page, or the appraiser).
- Value truth: only realized arm's-length sales (gross including the buyer's premium, adjusted for time to the valuation date), independent credentialed appraisals, and the time-split public lots.
- The founders' values are excluded from value scoring.
- Set a minimum count per category before any figure is quoted outside Havellin.

wrong.item: "Then publish the accuracy figure" and the one-page accuracy statement for trust officers
wrong.why: A published error rate is a representation. When one value later proves wrong, a beneficiary's counsel will put it in front of the court as the standard Havellin promised (negligent misrepresentation, FDUTPA). Zillow's figure rests on millions of sales; Havellin's would rest on hundreds at most, in categories that vary widely.

wrong.item: The positioning section's independence case: "Havellin never buys, Agent Two is never told where an item is going ... referral fees are disclosed"
wrong.why:
Three points undercut the claim.
- **The fees:** the channel Havellin chooses pays Havellin, which is *Kollsman*'s fact pattern.
- **The field note:** the crew's spoken note goes to Agent Two in full (`fieldNote` in `_avItemPayload`), and the plan's own living-jobs pack relies on notes that name the destination ("going to Karen"). So the claim that the agent never learns where a line is going is not true in every case.
- **The concierge:** can type over any figure after choosing the channel.
wrong.fix: Resolve the referral-fee question first (see the missing item). Fix the valuation-date figure when the schedule is adopted. Then state independence precisely: who values, when, and what they are paid by whom. Drop "never told where an item is going" from any client-facing claim unless destination words are stripped from the note before it is sent.

wrong.item: The plan's evidence standard ("The market where such a thing is most commonly sold to the public ... with the buyer's premium inside"), and the prompt it leaves standing
wrong.why:
Agent Two's prompt defines fair market value as "not retail, not an asking price". §20.2031-1(b) says the opposite for property the public buys at retail: there the value is the retail price, in the used market where the item is sold. For branded furniture and decor, that market is resale and consignment.

The buyer's premium belongs inside the figure only where auction is that market (*Scull*; PLR 9235005 [S]). LiveAuctioneers' results are hammer prices without the premium (R2 C).
wrong.fix:
In P12:
- Replace "It is not retail" with the regulation's rule, market by class: auction including the premium for art, antiques, silver and jewelry; used retail or resale for branded furniture, decor and electronics.
- Each basis names its market.
- Hammer-only comparables are labelled as such, or grossed up by the house's stated premium.

Counsel confirms the premium question for a non-tax Florida inventory (R1 D9).

wrong.item: The plan's answer on Etsy: "good evidence of what a thing is"
wrong.why:
On value, the plan is right: an asking price is a ceiling at most, never fair market value. On identity it gives a marketplace listing too much weight. A seller's attribution is the seller's guess, and origins are misstated in listings all the time. In the Ellison case a listing happened to be right.

If Agent Two overturns a name on the strength of a listing, the record ends up resting on a stranger's attribution.
wrong.fix: Identity rests on the mark read in a close-up, corroborated by a pattern reference (Replacements' identification pages, a maker's-mark library), or on an appraiser. A listing is a lead to that reference, never the evidence. Where a listing is Agent Two's only evidence, the basis says so and the line reads *unsure*.

wrong.item: When the agents disagree: "still with no new flag (Q95)"; the disagreement only counted in the score
wrong.why: A change of maker, origin, material or period is a change in the description the personal representative verifies under oath. Writing it in silently, with Agent One's reading "never printed", leaves a later reader unable to tell a guess from an identification.
wrong.fix: No new review tier. Where Agent Two changes the maker, origin, material or period, and the change does not rest on a mark it read or a reference match, the line shows the existing *unsure* hint until a person ticks it. The record shows both readings and the evidence for each. A correction resting on a legible mark goes in without a flag, as Q95 intends.

wrong.item: Ask 6: write "Havellin estimate · Ashley Jerome" automatically on any figure the concierge types
wrong.why: This hides the fact that there is no basis, which is exactly what §733.604(3) attacks. On the paper, a concierge's unsupported correction would read like a considered estimate, and it is the weakest value on the schedule.
wrong.fix: Below $500, write the automatic basis "Havellin estimate (staff)". At $500 or more (the line that gets its own initial), print "Havellin estimate: basis not stated" in amber until a person picks a reason or pastes a comparable. Valuation Support lists these lines. It is a flag, never a block.

wrong.item: Ask 19's second and third options ("say 'Havellin's estimates' without naming AI" / "nothing beyond today")
wrong.why:
These are not acceptable choices for what the fiduciary and counsel receive.
- Under §736.0807 the fiduciary must review the agent's work, which requires knowing the method.
- Under AO-41, leaving out the use of a tool is a problem wherever the omission would mislead.
- Concealment found later would cost more credibility than any disclosure.
wrong.fix: Disclosure to the fiduciary and counsel is required, through the engagement term and the methodology page. The only real question for counsel is the wording on the schedule as filed, which is the representative's own verified document.

wrong.item: Ask 5: an appraisal figure typed in before the report is filed goes FINAL, with "report to follow"
wrong.why: That is acceptable for a §733.604 schedule, which carries estimated values. It is not acceptable on a Form 706 estate, where the sworn appraisal must be attached to the return.
wrong.fix: Keep the recommendation off Form 706 estates. On a Form 706 estate the line reads "appraisal figure recorded; report not filed", and the 706 readiness list and the package's cover summary name it until the report is filed.

wrong.item: Ask 16 is too narrow ("signed art, designer jewelry, watches and named makers")
wrong.why: Value turns on authenticity or testing for all fine jewelry, gemstones, Asian ceramics and works of art (which R2 D.2(6) names), and period furniture. Those are the classes where a photograph-based estimate is weakest and a Palm Beach estate's value sits.
wrong.fix: On an estate: all fine jewelry (tested), Asian works of art, signed art, watches, named makers, and pieces described as period go to the appraiser whatever their figure. The agents name and estimate; they never attest.

wrong.item: Ask 27: "ask counsel first, then build it" (date-of-death value and gain or loss on the ledger)
wrong.why: Printing the inventory value beside the realized net is not accounting work. These are two numbers Havellin already holds, and a trust accounting asks for both values (R1 B2 [P]). Only the gain-or-loss column moves toward accounting.
wrong.fix: Print the inventory value and its basis beside the realized gross, fees and net on the ledger on every values tier, as part of P15's sales-against-values line. Leave gain or loss to the accountant, so counsel needs to be asked nothing.

wrong.item: The best-in-class section's framing ("The agents can have what no appraiser has ...") and the goal of beating a twenty-year appraiser

The order should follow what a fiduciary relies on: first the data is safe and confidential, then the paper is true, then it can be defended, then it is measured, and only then is it fast.

1. **P0 (new): lock down the backend** (see the missing item). It comes first, before any real estate's data goes in.
2. **P1 and P4: data losses.** As planned.
3. **P3, P2 and the first two items of P13: authority, firearms, the appraiser hand-off.**
4. **The papers made true: P5, P6, P8, P10, P11, P9.** Also, from P12, the market and standard correction (remove "not retail"; the premium only where auction is the market) and the basis-change and §2032 guards.
5. **Pulled forward into Phase 1, before any real estate receives a FINAL schedule:**
   - from P19: the preparer's statement with its limiting conditions and independence certification, the methodology page, and a minimal per-line Valuation Support (its comparables are already stored);
   - from P27: the rooms index on the paper;
   - the routing of every marked artistic or intrinsic article on a Form 706 estate;
   - the exempt-property and §20.2031-6(c) cautions;
   - the per-beneficiary summary;

7. **The launch gate's attorney read of the package.** It goes here, before any Phase 2 or Phase 3 build, so counsel's changes land once.
8. **P17 before P16 and P18.** Getting the mark photographed while the crew is in the house is the biggest accuracy lever: it is what would have settled the Ellison china without luck, and it costs no model.

review.verdict:
This is my professional judgement from both seats, the ASA appraiser's and the bank trust officer's. Built as drafted, the plan gives Havellin the best whole-house record in Palm Beach. Every article would be photographed, numbered, routed, approved in writing and reconciled to what it brought, faster than any auction house or liquidator works. That alone wins the household-contents work that trust departments now give to liquidators and move managers.

It would not yet beat a twenty-year appraiser, and nothing in it is built to prove that it does. Three reasons:

1. **The value sits in a few dozen items, and nobody who values them handles them.** Identification of those items rests on photographs behind a single gate. An ordinary lot reaches Agent Two as text unless Agent One hedged its name or left it ungraded (havellin.html:38573). Agent One's prompt files unmarked, store-bought-looking vases and decor as General/Household (main-sync.gs:3442). So one confident misreading of a sleeper is never looked at again before it goes to Goodwill.

2. **The accuracy programme would produce a number a careful attorney takes apart.** It grades the agents against a truth Anthony and Ashley set, on the one house the prompts were tuned on: the valuing prompt's worked example is the Ellison plates' own answer, "likely Spanish, Puente del Arzobispo type" (main-sync.gs:4452). It also scores against sale figures that leave out the buyer's premium, because the proceeds statement records only gross and fees.

3. **A trust department stops before it reads the inventory.** The jobs backend hands every client's record and inventory to anyone holding its URL (`doGet` loadJobs and loadMedia, main-sync.gs:141; MANUAL.md:83 says to deploy as Anyone). And Havellin takes referral fees from the channels that sell what it valued. That is the *Kollsman* pattern the plan's positioning holds against the auction houses.

Would I choose Havellin over the firm I use today?
- **The whole-house inventory, the release paperwork and the ledger:** yes, once Phase 1 makes every paper true and the backend is locked.
- **The values on the items that matter:** only with an independent, credentialed appraiser's name on them.

That combination is the winning model: Havellin catalogues and researches everything, and an appraiser with no stake in the sale reviews and signs, in days rather than weeks and at a fraction of today's fee. "Better than a twenty-year appraiser" is the wrong claim. "A twenty-year appraiser working from our catalogue, every basis on paper, with a measured error rate" is the claim that wins Palm Beach.

missing.title: A sleeper check before anything irreversible, on every job
missing.why: In this trade the costliest error is the valuable thing in the donation or dump load: an unmarked Chinese export vase read as decorator stock, a watch in a nightstand box, a print that is an original. Today one confident Agent One call decides whether anyone with research depth ever sees the photograph. Donate and Junk cannot be undone, and the plan's metrics would not even notice the miss, because the item never reaches a sale.
missing.proposal:
Two changes.
- Give every photographed line to Agent Two with its photograph. Anthony has said cost is not the concern.
- Before a Donate, Junk or Remove line leaves (when the disposition is set, and again when the pickup is signed out), give each line no agent has seen at research depth one photograph look. The question is narrow: could this be worth more than $250 an article, or need a specialist? Write a note only on a yes.

This adds no box and no second review tier; the line simply goes to research. Score it as "sleeper recall".

missing.why: A trust attorney will not put a move manager's AI estimates for the valuable lines in front of a court or the IRS without a credentialed name, and *Kollsman* is about precisely who stands behind a figure. Today an appraiser is linked only line by line, by threshold. Havellin's own agreement says its records "are not an appraisal or a statement of value", yet the Court Inventory carries Havellin's values.

Retain one or two ASA or ISA appraisers on a flat or hourly fee, with no interest in consigning or buying and no referral relationship. On each values-tier estate they either:
- review, under USPAP Standard 3, a stratified random sample of the agent figures and every line over $1,000; or
- sign a desktop Standard 8 report on the contents, naming Havellin's catalogue as significant assistance.

The schedule then reads "values reviewed by …, ASA". Price it as the appraiser's own vendor line, consistent with Q20. This is the single change that would make me switch firms.

missing.title: Record the buyer's premium, so Havellin's own sales can be the truth and an adopted sale is FMV
missing.why: A consignor's statement shows the hammer price less commission. Fair market value at auction includes the buyer's premium (*Scull*; PLR 9235005), typically 20 to 30%. The plan's P15 compares inventory values with the statement's gross and lets counsel adopt the sale price, so correct values will look high, adopted values will understate the schedule, and the scoring's best ground truth is biased. A last-day estate-sale tag price is orderly liquidation, not FMV.
missing.proposal: Record each auction vendor's buyer's premium in the Vendor Directory. On each sold line compute the buyer's price (hammer × (1 + premium)). P15 compares FMV with the buyer's price, and the adopt press adopts it, dated against the valuation date, with a note where the channel pays Havellin a referral fee. Record estate-sale results as their own market.

Appraisers' desktop estimates on ordinary goods vary widely too, so an agent error rate means nothing without the human rate beside it.

Score the agents and the appraisers against realised buyer's prices where they exist. The published claim is the comparison, stated with its n.

missing.title: Headline metrics that match the asymmetric risk
missing.why: A median error over a house is dominated by $20 lots. What hurts a fiduciary is a missed $20,000 item, a flat wrong attribution and a total that is materially off. The plan reports these late, or not at all.

Lead with three figures:
1. Sleeper recall: the share of items truly worth over $1,000 and over $3,000 that the pipeline sent to research or an appraiser (target near 100%).
2. Overclaim rate: flat, unhedged maker, origin or period calls that were wrong, with the hedge calibration (how often "likely" is right).

After those come the plan's median error, the ±25% and ±50% hit rates, the price-related differential and interval coverage by band.

missing.title: A close-up protocol by class, for the camera and Close-ups wanted
missing.why: The marks and construction that identify a thing are known by class, and the field guide's table leaves out the very classes §20.2031-6(b) names. Plan P17's Close-ups wanted has the mechanism but not this content.
missing.proposal:
Add rows to the guide, and drive Close-ups wanted from the same list:
- **Silver:** every hallmark; the underside; say "weighted" or "hollow handles".
- **Gold and jewelry:** the stamps on the clasp and shank, the maker, any GIA inscription.
- **Bronze and sculpture:** the signature and the foundry mark on the base.
- **Asian works of art:** the base and foot rim.
- **Furniture, for dating:** a drawer side showing the joint, the underside, the back panel.
- **Paintings:** a low-angle shot of the surface to tell paint from print, and the canvas edge.
- **Books:** the title page and the copyright page.
- **Coins:** both faces and the holder label.

Put a scale card in frame for art, rugs and case pieces.

Record one of four grades on each line: *mark read* (quoted), *reference match* (named and linked), *papers or provenance*, or *visual only*. Agent Two writes it, and Valuation Support prints it.
- A flat maker or origin prints only on the first three grades.
- When the agents disagree and neither read a mark, the name prints hedged with both readings ("tin-glazed earthenware, Spanish or Italian"), and the line goes on Close-ups wanted while the crew is still in the house.

This adds no flag and no new tier. The score counts disagreements by grade and who was right.

- household furnishings and up to two vehicles leaving before the §732.402 petition deadline (four months after notice of administration) where a spouse or children may claim them;

The plan does not mention either.

wrong.item: Ask 11's recommendation: Anthony and Ashley settle the truth for the Ellison set in about an evening.
wrong.why: Scores are only as good as their answer key. Two people who are not appraisers deciding what a thing is and what it is worth makes the agents agree with Havellin, not with the market. On the china they would have had to look it up the way Agent Two did. An attorney who asks "who says your answer key is right?" ends the accuracy statement.
wrong.fix: Value truth is a realised buyer's price (Havellin's own sales, with the premium added) and an appraiser's figure. Identification truth on the lines that matter is a paid independent appraiser's call. Anthony and Ashley's evening settles counts, rooms and destinations, and serves as a smoke test, never as the answer key.

wrong.item: Ellison as the golden set and the baseline (3(a) step 1, P15).
wrong.why: The prompts were tuned on Ellison. The valuing prompt's worked example is the Ellison plates' correct answer (main-sync.gs:4452), and the mirror, the shears and the Herend probe are Ellison lines (4361-4363, 4407, 4928, 4935). A score there measures what the prompt remembers.
wrong.fix: Call Ellison the development set and build the test set from houses never shown to the prompts, frozen and hidden from whoever edits them. See the held-out set under missing.

wrong.item: Setting targets "by category and by value band" from a 60 to 100 line set.
wrong.why: Thirteen categories by four bands leaves a handful of lines per cell. A ±25% hit rate on five lines is noise, and targets set on it will be wrong in both directions.
wrong.fix: Set targets only from several hundred lines with realised prices, stratified so each high-value class has at least 30, and print a confidence interval beside every figure.

wrong.item: The 200 to 300 public post-cutoff lots, with "each lot's own page" excluded.
wrong.why:
There are three problems.
- **Getting the photographs:** collecting them in bulk from LiveAuctioneers or Invaluable is the scraping the Decided list rules out.
- **Distribution shift:** catalogue photographs are lit, cleaned and described by a specialist, so scores on them flatter a crew's iPhone in a dark closet.
- **Leakage:** one lot's result appears on the house's site, the aggregators and the press, so hiding its own page does not hide it, and comparables dated after the sale leak the answer.
wrong.fix: Take the photographs under licence, or by hand within the sites' terms. Reject any run whose kept comparable is the lot itself on any site, or post-dates the valuation date. Report catalogue-photo and field-photo scores apart, and trust only the field ones.

wrong.item: Etsy listings as "good evidence of what a thing is".
wrong.why: Listing text is a seller's guess, and marketplaces misattribute maker, origin and period constantly. As I understand the tools (not confirmed in this session), Agent Two reads a fetched page's text, not its pictures, so "the exact same pattern" was a match on a stranger's words. It happened to be right.
wrong.fix: Identify from the mark read off Havellin's own close-up, checked against a standard mark reference or the pattern's reference page (Replacements, by agreement). A listing counts toward identity only if its photographs show the same mark. Asking prices print, if at all, only in Valuation Support, marked "asking, not relied on".

wrong.item: P15's "Sales against inventory value" and "Counsel can adopt an arm's-length sale price in one press", read off the statement's gross.
wrong.why: A consignor statement's gross is the hammer price, while FMV at auction includes the buyer's premium. Correct values will be flagged as high, an adopted sale will understate the schedule by 20 to 30%, and a last-day estate-sale price is liquidation, not FMV.
wrong.fix: Record each vendor's premium and compare and adopt the buyer's price, dated against the valuation date, noting any referral-fee channel. See the premium item under missing.

wrong.item: Silver and gold "valued no lower than melt at spot on the value date".
wrong.why: No refiner pays full melt at spot. A lot's weighable silver excludes stainless knife blades, filled handles and weighted bases, which can be most of a piece's weight. Continental 800 or 830 and coin silver are not sterling. A gross-weight melt floor overstates the value.
wrong.fix: The floor is the weighable precious metal, by purity, at a typical refiner's payout on the value date, and it is never offered as the FMV. The crew says "weighted" or "hollow handles" at the camera.

wrong.item: Ask 6's recommendation: write "Havellin estimate · Ashley Jerome" as the basis automatically.
wrong.why: A name is not a basis. §733.604(3) entitles a beneficiary to how a value was determined; this answers who, and turns the honest red "not stated" into a false answer.
wrong.fix: Offer one tap from a short list when a figure is typed: a comparable sale (paste the link), Havellin's own sale of a like item, the going rate for the lot, a condition adjustment to the agent's figure, or an appraiser's verbal opinion. The person's name rides beside the basis, not in place of it.

wrong.item: Ask 16: route authenticity-dependent items to an appraiser "on an estate", for "signed art, designer jewelry, watches and named makers".
wrong.why: "Named makers" sweeps in every Pottery Barn lamp, while the list leaves out Asian works of art, bronzes, couture handbags and coins, which are the classes most often reproduced. Limiting it to estates is the wrong cut: a living client who donates a Qing vase or sells a fake Rolex through Havellin's channel loses as much, and Havellin is the one explaining it.
wrong.fix: Route by class and by irreversibility on every job: signed fine art, precious jewelry, luxury watches and handbags, Asian works of art, bronzes and attributed period antiques, whatever the figure, whenever the line is to be sold, donated or junked.

wrong.item: "High" confidence on "three or more sales within three years of the value date that bracket the figure".
wrong.why: China patterns, crystal, brown furniture and figurines, the bulk of a Palm Beach house, have fallen hard, so a three-year-old sale overstates them. The 2026-10-26 Herend probe rested on a 2015 Bonhams sale and two eBay asking prices. Bracketing proves nothing unless the sales match on pattern, size and condition. eBay "Best Offer accepted" listings show the list price, not the price paid.
wrong.fix: High needs three sold matches on maker, pattern or model, size and condition, within a recency set by category (12 to 18 months for falling classes) or time-adjusted with the adjustment stated. Treat a Best Offer sale as sold with the price not shown.

wrong.item: P18's two-model second opinion read as independent evidence ("within 25% the median is used").
wrong.why: Two models running the same searches find the same comparables and anchor on the same top result. Their agreement is correlated, so a 25% spread rule misses the case where both are wrong together.
wrong.fix: Make the second pass blind and different: other sources (licensed data where it exists), no shared comparables, no first figure. On the top band, use the independent appraiser rather than another model.

wrong.item: Positioning: "independence: Havellin never buys, Agent Two is never told where an item is going … referral fees are disclosed."
wrong.why: A trust officer applies *Kollsman* to Havellin too: the firm that values an item and chooses its channel takes a fee from that channel. A disclosure in the agreement is not consent after fair disclosure by every interested person (§733.610; R1 D5). And no paper that states a value carries the disclosure.
wrong.fix: Disclose on the valuation papers, lock and date each value before the channel is chosen, and put the estate-credit question to Anthony (a revisit of Q62). See missing.

wrong.item: "Then publish the accuracy figure" / a one-page accuracy statement "once the numbers are real".
wrong.why: A self-graded figure, measured on sales through channels Havellin chose and is paid by, is discoverable in litigation, easy to attack, and reads as a warranty.
wrong.fix: Publish only after an independent appraiser has reviewed a random sample and the head-to-head with appraisers has run. Counsel words it, and n and the intervals are stated.

wrong.item: The verdict's opening: "The desk is already ahead of how anyone in Palm Beach does this work."
wrong.why: That is true of completeness, speed and reconciliation. It is not true at the top of the house, where a specialist holding the object catches the sleeper, the married piece and the reproduction. Believing the claim internally leads to under-routing.
wrong.fix: Say the desk is ahead on the record and behind on handling the valuable few, and close the gap with the sleeper check and the appraiser partnership.
